M. Shamsul Alam, D.A.C. with Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, M. A Rouf, Advocates ------ For the State.

parties:

 Vs.
Manik Bala ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
9. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahman Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf on the condemned prisoner has submitted that there is no direct evidence of the murder in this case. The learned Advocate submitted that the confessional statement of the condemned prisoner was neither voluntary nor true inasmuch as the condemned prisoner retracted from his confessional statement alleging torture by the police. He further submitted that the prosecution failed to prove that the confessional statement was true. The learned Advocate also contended that the learned Sessions Judge has committed an error of law in admit-ting the statement of Sona Barn recorded under section 164 Cr.P.C. into evidence and for relying upon the same as a corroboration of the statements of the condemned prisoner in his confession. 

 10. Mr. M. Shamsul Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, on the other hand, has submit-ted that the confessional statement of the condemned prisoner was voluntary and true and that the accused could be convicted upon his confessional statement alone. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, however, candidly conceded that the learned Sessions Judge wrongly admitted the statement of Sona Baru into evidence. 

 11. As to the contention of the learned Advocate for the condemned prisoner that the statement of the mother of the condemned prisoner recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not admissible in evidence. The learned Deputy Attorney-General did not dispute the legal proposition. It is now well settled that a statement recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be admitted as a substantive evidence against the accused person it can only be used for the purpose of contradicting or corroborating the maker of the statement. The prosecution, however, is entitled to use the statement recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to impeach the credibility of the maker if examined as a witness and also where a witness resiles from his statement recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the purpose of prosecuting him for perjury but it is not relevant against the accused in any manner whatsoever. 

 14. So far as the confessional statement is concerned the prosecution adduced evidence in sup-port of the fact that accused Manik was with the de-ceased at the place of occurrence (house) and that after committing the murder he fled away with the sari and sponge sandal of his wife. As to the statement of his mother Ext.2 it is not admissible in evidence and as such the learned Sessions Judge has committed an error of law in admitting the same into evidence and relying upon the same for his decision. As to the recovery and seizure of the sari and the sponge sandal it is quite improbable that P.W.4, a member of the Union Parishad who went to the bazar to purchase some betel nut will take the sari and the sponge sandal from the mother of the accused; nor it is probable that mother of the accused Manik will hand over the sari and the sandal to P.W.4. Further it appears that one Nurul Huque who produced the sari and the sponge sandal before the officer-in-charge was not examined nor is there any evidence to show that the said sari and the sponge sandal belonged to the wife of the accused Manik. The identity of those articles were not established by the prosecution. 

 15. So far as the promise of payment of money is concerned, it appears to be improbable in view of the positive evidence of P.W.2 himself that at the time of marriage of his daughter with accused Manik the accused transferred 40 decimals of land in favour of Alo Tara. As such there could be no question of any payment of money by the father of Alo Tara to the accused Manik. Although the prosecution examined P.W.3 to prove that accused Manik came to the house of the informant on 13.8.85 in the evening, no other witness was examined in support of this fact. Tozamber Ali who awakened the informant from sleep and who accompanied him to the police station to lodge the F.I.R. was not examined. 

 16. It appears that the accused retracted from his confessional statement by filing a petition on 29.11.85 and in his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure he also retracted from his confessional statement alleging torture by the Police. He stated in his statement recorded under section 342 Cr.P.C. that he gifted 40 decimals of land to his wife Alo Tara at the time of his marriage with her ; that his father-in-law told him about a Salish which was hei,2 over the dispute of payment of Tk.5000/- to his father-in-law for the purchase of his land by his cousin brothers and that at the Salish accused Serajul Hoque refused to pay money to his father-in-law and had also beaten his father-in-law with shoes. He also stated about some case instituted by him against Abul Hossain and others. It thus appears that the accused has retracted from his confessional statement wherein he stated that he took part in the murder of Alo Tara and Abdus Sukur along with 4 others. The prosecution story and the story in the confessional statement are not the same. They differ in material particulars. There is positive evidence of P.W.2 that the marriage between his daughter and accused Manik was blissful one and there can be no reason for the accused to murder his wife and his brother-in-law. Furthermore, he was looking after the interest of his father-in-law and filed a case before the Upazila Chairman on his behalf. 

 17. Apart from the confessional statement the prosecution failed to prove the charge of murder against the condemned prisoner by adducing any reliable evidence- The sheet anchor of the prosecution is the confessional statement which was retracted by the accused. Reading the statement between the lines it appears that bulk of the statement made therein are inconsistent and improbable with human nature and cannot be accepted as true statement of fact. The prosecution took no step to establish by adducing evidence that there was, in fact, a Salish held on 13.8.85 over the dispute for non payment of money by accused Seraj to the informant. None of the wit-nesses mentioned about the salish as stated in the confessional statement.' The prosecution took no step to prove that the confessional statement was true. The manner in which the murder was alleged to have been committed is not free from doubt although there is no dispute that the two victims were strangulated to death and them is no challenge to the evidence of the doctor in this regard. 

 18. In order to convict a person charged with murder there should be unimpeachable evidence of re-liable witnesses bringing home the guilt of the accused beyond any reasonable doubt. The burden is certainly on the prosecution to establish its case whether that burden has been discharged or not by the prosecution should be decided on the facts of the case as a whole and if in dealing with the whole case a reasonable doubt arises then the benefit of that doubt be given to the accused. 

 19. The confessional statement as against its maker is supposed to be the best evidence; but when a confession is made the foundation for conviction, the Court must be satisfied that it is true and voluntary. The truth or falsity of a confessional statement has to be weighed by the Court in the light of all the facts and surrounding circumstances of the case. Normally it would not be quite safe as a matter of prudence to base a conviction for murder on the basis of a retracted confession alone when the confession is open to a good deal of criticism specially when the proof of the factum of murder is itself solely dependent upon a confession. 

 20. In the instant case before us the prosecution started with the improbable story of a demand of Tk.2000/- by the accused from his father-in-law which is improbable on the face of it as it is admit-ted by the informant himself that the accused gifted 40 decimals of land to his daughter at the time of her marriage. The confessional statement itself reveals that there were sounds and cries at the time of com-mission of the murder but the prosecution adduced no evidence in support of that fact. Rather the prosecution tried to prove the recovery of a sari and a pair of sponge sandals alleged to have been carried by the accused from the place of occurrence which is improbable in the facts and circumstances of the case nor it is probable that the mother of the accused would hand over the sari and the sponge sandal to the member of a Union Parishad and at the top of it the prosecution failed to establish that the sari and the sponge sandal belonged to deceased Alo Tara. Moreover, the learned Sessions Judge found the confession-al statement to be false as against the co-accused Seraj. Hence there is a break in the chain of the prosecution story leaving ample scope for reasonable doubt. Moreover, the version of events given in the confessional statement is not only highly improbable but the facts stated therein were not corroborated by any other evidence and as such it will be unsafe to base a conviction for murder on such a confessional statement. A retracted confession is always open to suspicion and cannot be acted upon unless it is corroborated by credible independent evidence. We are, therefore, constrained to hold that the prosecution has not been able to bring home the charge
